clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic CYP7B1 variants that disrupt oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase in the acidic bile-acid synthesis pathway

Often a relatively pure phenotype of progressive lower-limb spasticity and weakness, but complicated forms with sensory disturbance, sphincter symptoms, optic changes or white-matter lesions are well described
Age at onset is broad, ranging from early childhood to mid-adult life, sometimes within the same family
Markedly raised plasma 27-hydroxycholesterol (and often 25-hydroxycholesterol) is a biochemical hallmark and a useful pointer to the diagnosis
Brain and cord MRI may show white-matter signal change and thinning of the thoracic cord, supporting a complicated presentation
Accumulated oxysterols are neurotoxic, and interest exists in cholesterol-lowering or bile-acid strategies, though disease-modifying benefit is unproven
Management is symptomatic and multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, spasticity control and gait aids, with bladder and mood support as needed
reference.pathophysiology: SPG5 arises from loss-of-function variants in CYP7B1, which encodes oxysterol 7-alpha-hydroxylase, a cytochrome P450 enzyme in the alternative (acidic) pathway of bile-acid synthesis. Impaired enzyme activity causes accumulation of neurotoxic oxysterols such as 27-hydroxycholesterol, which are thought to injure long corticospinal and sensory axons and to promote oxidative and lipid-handling stress within neurons. The resulting length-dependent axonal degeneration produces the characteristic slowly progressive spastic paraparesis, with variable dorsal-column sensory and white-matter involvement in more complicated cases.
additionalDifferentials: Other autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegias (SPG7, SPG11, SPG15)
Cerebrotendinous xanthomatosis and other inborn errors of sterol metabolism
Dopa-responsive dystonia presenting with spastic gait
Primary progressive multiple sclerosis with a spinal presentation
Vitamin B12 or copper deficiency myelopathy
Tropical spastic paraparesis and compressive cervical myelopathy
additionalInvestigations: Molecular testing of CYP7B1, ideally within a hereditary spastic paraplegia gene panel
MRI of brain and whole spine to assess white matter and cord thinning
Nerve conduction studies and evoked potentials to characterise axonal or sensory involvement
Very-long-chain fatty acids and plasma sterols to exclude mimics
Serum vitamin B12, copper and inflammatory or infective myelopathy screen where appropriate
redFlags: Rapid deterioration or a sensory level suggesting a compressive or inflammatory myelopathy rather than a genetic cause
New visual failure indicating optic pathway involvement needing ophthalmology review
Sphincter disturbance with retention requiring urological assessment
Cognitive decline or seizures suggesting a more widespread leukodystrophy-like process
reference.prognosis: SPG5 is typically slowly progressive, and many affected individuals remain ambulant for years, although some eventually require walking aids; complicated presentations with prominent white-matter disease may progress more noticeably.
pitfalls: Overlooking the diagnosis because the phenotype can look like a pure HSP without distinctive features
Not measuring oxysterols, which can provide a rapid and specific biochemical clue
Assuming a sporadic case cannot be recessive when parents are unaffected carriers
Attributing progressive spasticity to multiple sclerosis without genetic and metabolic testing
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Symptomatic antispasticity therapy with baclofen or tizanidine, and botulinum toxin for focal spasticity

Consideration of cholesterol-lowering statin therapy and/or chenodeoxycholic acid to lower neurotoxic oxysterols such as 27-hydroxycholesterol, recognising that disease-modifying benefit remains unproven and use is confined to trials or specialist settings
Regular physiotherapy, stretching and provision of orthoses and walking aids to maintain gait
Bladder care with urodynamic assessment and antimuscarinic therapy for sphincter symptoms
Monitoring of the plasma oxysterol profile and MRI white-matter and cord change, with surveillance for complicated sensory or optic features
Genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance with carrier testing of relatives
